content: To eliminate rabies as a public health problem, a country must demonstrate zero human deaths from rabies over a continuous 24-month period. Rabies must also be a notifiable disease in both humans and animals. The country must provide evidence of the following: 1. An effective national strategy for rabies control and elimination. 2. A reduction in the number of dog rabies cases as a result of implementing the national rabies control and elimination strategy. 3. A decrease in human deaths from rabies due to the implementation of the national rabies control and elimination strategy. If a country can verify the interruption of dog-mediated rabies transmission, it is also considered to have validated the elimination of rabies as a public health problem. Annex 14 provides a draft template for the documentation required to validate achieving zero human deaths from rabies. Verification of rabies transmission interruption involves demonstrating the absence of animal cases caused by canine rabies virus variants for at least 24 months. Evidence must also be provided for: A post-elimination strategy or contingency plan that ensures access to dog vaccines and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) procedures, as well as surveillance and epidemiological investigation of any reintroduction of rabies from other regions or countries. A reduction in dog-mediated animal rabies cases to zero, attributed to the implementation of the national rabies elimination strategy. Maintenance of zero dog-mediated human rabies cases. Given the time required for verification, countries are encouraged to first self-declare freedom from dog-mediated rabies in accordance with OIE procedures. The documentation for OIE self-declaration will then be reviewed to verify that rabies transmission has been interrupted. Annex 14 outlines the proposed dossier template for verifying the interruption of rabies transmission. Since rabies was identified as a priority by WHO, FAO, and OIE in 2011, it has become a model for a coordinated One Health approach between human and animal health sectors. This commitment was renewed in 2017 with the launch of an updated tripartite concept note. In 2015, WHO and OIE, in collaboration with FAO and the Global Alliance for Rabies Control (GARC), organized a global rabies conference in Geneva. This conference brought together stakeholders from veterinary and human health sectors, governments, and the private sector. It also launched the Global Framework for the Elimination of Dog-Mediated Human Rabies, which outlines the actions required to achieve the goal of zero human rabies deaths worldwide by 2030. Numerous partners contribute to the prevention, control, and elimination of rabies at global, regional, and national levels. These include organizations such as ASEAN, the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, Humane Society International, Mission Rabies, Vets Beyond Borders, World Animal Protection, and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. These partners assist in developing global standards and policies, mobilizing resources, coordinating regional efforts, and directly supporting national programs. WHO plays a central role in setting global norms and standards, engaging stakeholders, and supporting countries in rabies control and elimination. It facilitates data collection on human rabies cases worldwide and collaborates with OIE to harmonize reporting systems for animal and human rabies. Between 2009 and 2015, WHO managed rabies elimination pilot programs funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation in South Africa, Tanzania, and the Philippines. Lessons learned from these projects are now being applied to international initiatives to accelerate rabies control. Since the launch of the Global Framework, WHO has been working with partners to develop a global strategic plan to end human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030. This plan includes a country-centric approach, with international partners supporting and empowering national entities to control and eliminate rabies. In 2017, WHO revised its position on rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins, providing updated recommendations to improve access to affordable rabies biologics, particularly for underserved populations. The updated intradermal PEP regimen is estimated to allow treatment of nearly 500 additional patients for every 1,000 vials of rabies vaccine compared to traditional intramuscular regimens. WHO is building the evidence base for including human rabies vaccines in Gavi's 2018 Vaccine Investment Strategy. If successful, this would ensure subsidized access to human rabies vaccines in lowand middle-income Gavi-eligible countries. In 2013, Gavi evaluated the feasibility, public health impact, and cost of improving access to rabies PEP in low-income settings in Africa and Asia. Studies conducted in over 20 countries identified challenges such as limited availability and supply of PEP, underreporting of rabies cases, lack of regular monitoring of PEP use, and patients not seeking or completing PEP. Stock-outs were common due to low budget allocation, ineffective use of PEP at treatment centers, and inaccurate vaccine forecasting. In all countries, these projects triggered additional activities, such as updating national rabies strategies, improving rabies reporting and surveillance systems, and strengthening laboratory networks. WHO regional offices, such as the South-East Asia Regional Office, have been proactive in preparing standards and guidelines, issuing recommendations, and providing technical support to member states for rabies prevention and control. They advocate for cost-effective intradermal vaccination to improve the availability and affordability of modern rabies vaccines and the phasing out of nerve tissue vaccines, which have now been abandoned in several countries. The ASEAN regional elimination strategy aims to eliminate human rabies in the region by 2020 through progressive control of dog rabies and human prophylaxis in endemic countries while maintaining rabies-free areas. WHO collaborates with ASEAN, FAO, and OIE to provide technical support for developing and implementing this strategy. Similar efforts are underway in South Asia, where WHO works with the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation to advocate for regionally coordinated rabies control activities. In the Americas, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) initiated a program in 1983 to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies. The program initially targeted principal cities in Latin America and later expanded to include rural areas. Since its inception, the program has achieved a more than 90% reduction in human and canine rabies cases in the Americas. It prioritized surveillance, improved access to human prophylaxis, mass dog vaccination, and good governance. PAHO member states can procure high-quality human rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins through the PAHO revolving fund. In 2015, canine rabies vaccines were also included in the fund for use in mass dog vaccination campaigns. Every two years, PAHO convenes a meeting of national program directors to discuss and update strategies for rabies prevention and control. Recommendations from these meetings are submitted to ministers of health and agriculture for endorsement during high-level inter-American ministerial meetings. The plan of action for eliminating dog-mediated human rabies in the Americas by 2022 or earlier is part of the broader effort to eliminate neglected infectious diseases. WHO collaborating centers strengthen the institutional capacity of member states by providing information, services, research, and training for rabies-related activities, including diagnosis, surveillance, and monitoring of elimination programs. There are 14 designated WHO collaborating centers for rabies research, located in Asia, Europe, and the Americas. These centers are officially designated by WHO based on a jointly agreed work plan, which is renewable after annual performance evaluations. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) contributes to rabies control by raising awareness, providing policy advice, and offering technical support for animal rabies control. It supports the establishment of animal health clubs in schools and focuses on the impact of rabies on livestock production. FAO has organized global stakeholder consultations to assist countries in identifying their needs for rabies control and has sent missions to control rabies outbreaks in countries like Indonesia and Vietnam. It also strengthens diagnostic capacity through its reference centers and networks, conducts proficiency testing, and provides training on dog population management. The World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) issues science-based standards and guidelines for improving animal health and welfare. It promotes responsible dog ownership and provides a global online notification system for reporting animal rabies. OIE also supports veterinary services through laboratory twinning programs and a network of reference laboratories and collaborating centers.
